facts.fact_text: On 6 March 2005 the applicant took part in a demonstration to mark the Women's Day celebrations in Beyazıt Square in Istanbul.

When the crowds began to disperse after the Women's Day celebrations on 6 March 2005, police officers started hitting people, including the applicant, with their truncheons and the ends of their weapons.
When the crowds began to disperse after the Women's Day celebrations on 6 March 2005, police officers sprayed people, including the applicant, with tear gas.
As a result of blows to her head, face and other parts of her body, the applicant fell to the ground during the incident on 6 March 2005.
Whilst the applicant was on the ground, police officers continued to kick and hit her with their sticks.
Police officers swore at the applicant and insulted her during the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant was seriously injured during the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant was left semi-conscious as a result of the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant had to be helped by a member of the public to leave the area after the incident on 6 March 2005.

Section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising board.

Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) prohibits demonstrations and processions on public streets, in parks, places of worship and buildings in which public services are based.

Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations organised in public squares must comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.

Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations and processions which do not comply with the provisions of the Act will be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators have been warned.

Section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911), as it read before it was amended in 2008 and 2010, provided that unarmed persons taking part in an unlawful meeting or procession who, instead of dispersing of their own motion after having been warned or ordered to do so and who thus have to be forcefully dispersed by government forces, are liable to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of between one and three years.

Section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911), as it read before it was amended in 2008 and 2010, provided that unless their action breaches another criminal law provision which stipulates a more severe punishment, persons who resort to violence or making threats while being dispersed, or who resist the attempts to disperse them, are liable to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of between three and five years.

Section 245 of the Criminal Code in force at the material time (Law No. 765) provided that any law-enforcement officer who, in the course of duty and in circumstances other than those prescribed by law, ill-treats, injures or hits a person or inflicts on them bodily harm, shall be sentenced to between three months' and five years' imprisonment and temporarily barred from public service.
Members of the security forces told people gathering on 6 March 2005 that they would not be allowed to march towards Beyazıt Square because it would obstruct the flow of traffic.
Those demonstrators who remained on 6 March 2005 blocked the traffic and insisted on marching to Beyazıt Square.
Members of the security forces intervened on 6 March 2005 and reopened the road that had been blocked by demonstrators.

Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations organised in public squares must comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.
When the police warned the group of approximately sixty persons who refused to leave Beyazıt Square, the demonstrators responded by throwing stones at the police officers.
As a result of demonstrators throwing stones at police officers, the police officers arrested a number of the demonstrators and took them into custody by using force.
The video footage shows police officers wearing gas masks hitting with their truncheons a large number of demonstrators who try to run away from the area.
The video footage shows demonstrators who had fallen to the ground being kicked and hit with truncheons by police officers.
The video footage shows a male demonstrator who uses his body to protect a woman on the ground being kicked in the face by a police officer.
The video footage shows police officers spraying demonstrators hiding in bushes with tear gas before hitting them with their truncheons.
The video footage shows two women on the ground trying to protect themselves from attacks by police officers being sprayed with tear gas.
The video footage shows women who had taken refuge in nearby shops and cafes being dragged out by the police and beaten up.

The video footage shows a number of shoppers, shopkeepers and other persons who had not been demonstrating but who had been in the area and were affected by the intense tear gas, wandering around in a confused state.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, police officers had not issued any warnings to the demonstrators to disperse before attacking them on 6 March 2005.
According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, the demonstrators had not resisted the police intervention on 6 March 2005.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, the demonstrators had not attacked the police on 6 March 2005 but had simply tried to run away from the area.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, police had hit the demonstrators — including those who had fallen to the ground — with their truncheons, kicked them, punched them and sprayed them with tear gas on 6 March 2005.

The defendant police officers maintained before the trial court that the demonstrators had been harming public order by insisting on continuing with the reading out of their press release and by attacking the police with iron bars.
The defendant police officers maintained before the trial court that the force used by them against the demonstrators had not been disproportionate.

The trial court found that in the Saraçhane area, the police did not interfere in the demonstration until the demonstrators started walking on the road where there was traffic circulation, and that intervention was made with a view to maintaining public order.

The trial court found that the video footage shows police intervention against people who had already surrendered themselves to the police or who had been hiding in bushes after having been sprayed with tear gas, occurring not on the road but off it.
The trial court found that in Beyazıt Square, the video footage shows a scuffle between the police and demonstrators carrying banners.

The trial court found that the video footage shows the police kicking and hitting with their truncheons and shields persons — mostly women — who try to run away from the scene and who are not carrying any banners, in Beyazıt Square.
The trial court found that some of the defendant police officers exceeded the limits of their powers on the use of force and used excessive force.
During the demonstration on 6 March 2005 in Beyazıt Square, police officers did not interfere with the demonstrations.
The Women's Day celebrations on 6 March 2005 ended with a press release issued by a number of women's organisations.

Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that assistance and medical aid are rendered to any injured or affected persons at the earliest possible moment.

Principle 5 of the Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials (Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, Havana, 1990) provides that whenever the lawful use of force and firearms is unavoidable, law enforcement officials shall ensure that relatives or close friends of the injured or affected person are notified at the earliest possible moment.

Paragraph 16 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Denmark (CAT/C/DNK/CO/5, 16 July 2007) recommends that Denmark ensure prompt and impartial investigations into all complaints or allegations of misconduct, in particular when a person dies or is seriously injured following contact with law enforcement officials.

Paragraph 16 of the Concluding observations of the UN Committee against Torture on Denmark (CAT/C/DNK/CO/5, 16 July 2007) recommends that Denmark review and strengthen its education and training programmes relating to the use of force by law enforcement officials to ensure that the use of force is strictly limited to that required to perform their duties.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that during the demonstration marking international Women's Day in Istanbul on 6 March 2005, police intervened with disproportionate force, using tear gas and truncheons and injuring a number of participants.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that the Turkish government quickly conveyed the message that such behaviour on the part of the police is unacceptable following the incident of 6 March 2005.

In its 2005 Progress Report on Turkey (COM (2005) 561 final), the European Commission stated that following the incident of 6 March 2005, the Ministry of Interior demoted and fined 6 policemen and reprimanded 3 senior officials.
